title: Fit a spin-on oil filter: gasket contact, then three quarters to one turn by hand, not left loose or cranked on
context: Lube technicians and mechanics fit spin-on oil filters every day (O*NET 49-3093.00, Tire and Lube Technicians; 49-3023.00, Automotive Service Technicians and Mechanics). Filter makers print it on the can: spin the filter on until its gasket contacts the base, then tighten it a further three quarters of a turn by hand (some say three quarters to one turn). A filter left at contact or a little past it works loose under engine vibration and leaks oil, while one cranked on well past a full turn crushes its gasket, which can roll out of its groove and blow out under oil pressure, and the filter cannot be removed by hand at the next change. Here a new filter has been started on the thread of a filter head bolted to the bench and stops three quarters of a turn short of gasket contact.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A die-cast aluminum remote oil filter mount (filter head) is bolted to the bench with four bolts: a block 7.5 cm deep (x), 9 cm wide (y) and 3.4 cm tall, with a round machined gasket land 7.2 cm across and 0.6 cm tall on top, so the gasket face is at z 4. Its threaded M20 x 1.5 nipple points straight up at x 30, y -12. Its two hose ports, on its left and right sides, are closed with gray plastic plugs, and a black witness line is painted on the front of the land and block. A new spin-on oil filter, 250 g, is threaded onto the nipple: a black painted steel can 6.6 cm across and 7 cm tall with a plain flat top, grip flutes around its top edge, a white printed band, a black rubber gasket on its base, a printed index stripe down its side (white on the black, black across the band), and three black quarter-turn ticks on the band. The thread is right-handed (tightens clockwise seen from above) and advances 1.5 mm per turn. The filter starts about five turns onto the nipple and three quarters of a turn (270 degrees) short of gasket contact, its gasket about 1.1 mm above the land and its index stripe facing left; at gasket contact the stripe faces the robot, lined up with the witness line. Nothing else is on the bench.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run and measures the filter's angle from gasket contact, positive when tightened past it (it starts at -270 degrees). Two mistakes score 0 and are irreversible: the filter coming off its thread at any point (unscrewed five turns), and the filter ever being tightened more than 450 degrees (1.25 turns) past contact, which crushes the gasket even if it is backed off. The score is also 0 if the filter ends under 90 degrees past contact (a third of the least any maker asks), or if more than 45 degrees of the new ground it gained past contact was not turned by a holding hand's own wrist. A hand holds the filter when its fingers are closed on the can (opening from 15 % of full travel tighter to 3 % looser than the can's width) with the tool point within 1.5 cm of the can's axis, anywhere from 1 cm above the gasket face to 1.5 cm above the top (the pad tips sit 1.3 cm below it). Each step, a hand holding it at either end of the step credits only as much turning as its wrist rolled clockwise (at most 30 degrees carried ahead of the filter), so a swipe, a knock, the other arm, or a hand merely around the can earns nothing, and turning back and forth over the same angles counts once; the 45 degrees cover the filter settling as the hand lets go. Otherwise: 0.25 for 90 to 180 degrees (partly tightened); 0.5 for 180 to 240 (under the makers' figure) or for 360 to 450 or ever past 360 (past the most any maker allows); 1.0 for 240 to 360 and never past 360, the makers' three quarters to one turn less 30 degrees for judging it by hand. Any score is capped at 0.5 while a hand is still on the filter (fingers under 85 % open with the tool point within 1.5 cm of the can), since the job ends with it let go. Full credit also needs both arms back home and still (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started, the arm's 1.6 cm tracking lag plus margin, and moving under 2 cm/s), so the bench is clear for the next job; 0.9 if not. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, mark the gasket-contact line across the can and head before the trial and tape a protractor ring with 15-degree marks around the land; afterwards read the stripe's angle against it, count whole turns from the video, and photograph it from above. Watch the video for a swiped spin and for the hand letting go.
reset_notes: Unscrew the filter, wipe and re-oil its gasket, spin it back on to gasket contact, check the witness lines meet, and back it off three quarters of a turn. Replace the filter if it was tightened past a full turn (its gasket is deformed).
fidelity: True size; the filter points up so a straight-down grip reaches it (some remote mounts carry it so). The thread is modeled: a slide coupled to a hinge, 1.5 mm per turn, and past gasket contact a turning friction growing 0.1 N·m per radian (capped at 1 N·m) that never turns the filter by itself, against about 15 to 20 N·m by hand in reality, so contact shows mainly visually. No oil, gasket deformation or leak is simulated.
